newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China gets double confidence booster pre-handover.
newsitem.headline: China gets double confidence booster pre-handover.

text.p: China on Wednesday received a double confidence booster just before it takes over Hong Kong after the United States renewed its trade privileges and decided to attend the swearing in of Hong Kong's new legislature.
The spectre of superpower trade isolation was banished for another year when the House of Representatives voted by a hefty margin to renew China's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) status.

"The right way to encourage further progress in China is not to cut China off but to draw China in," said President Bill Clinton, signalling a boost to trade between the world's most powerful and most populous nations.
The decisive move was hailed in Hong Kong, whose economy and stock market have been booming in the run-up to the handover to Beijing at midnight on June 30.
"It's great news, the MFN season is always unpredictable," said Mitch Presnick, a partner with Warren Williams International Public Affairs Consultant.

Hong Kong would have been seriously injured if China, which takes over on Tuesday after 150 years of British rule, had lost its MFN status. The territory, the world's seventh biggest trading economy, stood to lose up to $30 billion a year in related revenues.

MFN critics had said the benefits should be denied because of fears that China would erode Hong Kong's liberties and because of China's human rights record, trade imbalance with the United States and tensions with Taiwan.
But White House security adviser Samuel Berger argued that isolationism was counter-productive. "We cannot ignore a quarter of the world's people," he said.

Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is flying to Hong Kong for the handover but boycotting the swearing in of Beijing's handpicked provisional legislature which takes control of the new Chinese region under a "one country, two systems" formula.
But the United States said it would still be represented at the controversial ceremony, which Britain has boycotted.

An official explained that pragmatism had prevailed. Richard Boucher, the U.S. consul general in Hong Kong, will attend because "he has to work, for better or worse, with the new legislature. For practical reasons, he will go."

But Albright issued a warning to Beijing, saying that its handling of Hong Kong would act as a barometer for Sino-U.S. relations. She wants to underline U.S. support for democracy and free markets in Hong Kong.
In the dying days of Britain's empire east of Suez, the colony's lame duck legislature sought on Tuesday to head off any Chinese crackdown by passing laws minimising punishment for political dissent.
Tung Chee-hwa, the billionaire shipping magnate who takes over control of one of the world's most successful free markets on July 1, rejected the legislature's moves.
"We will not accept these amendments which are themselves confusing," he said.

Martin Lee, the voice of democracy in Hong Kong, said he was ready to risk jail by scaling the walls of the Legislative Council building if Beijing blocked protests on the night of the handover when the world will be watching.

He called the new legislature a Beijing puppet chamber and said Chinese rule would strangle development in Hong Kong, which has enjoyed an annual growth rate of up to six percent a year over the past decade.
"China is putting a noose around the neck of the goose so the goose cannot be free but China still expects the goose to lay the golden egg," he said.
